title: Why Miners Took Canaries Underground
topic: Why coal miners carried canaries underground

lines: A coal miner carried a small bird deep underground.
The bird rode in a cage, breathing faster than any man.
The miner trusted this tiny creature with his life.
The mine air could hide carbon monoxide, a gas with no smell.
Miners could not see it, smell it, or feel it.
One breath of enough gas could stop a man's heart.
You see, it's like a smoke detector beeping before you see flames.
Canaries breathe faster and have a higher metabolism than miners.
Their small bodies absorbed the poison first.
The bird would collapse while the miners still felt fine.
That collapse gave miners time to escape.
The bird's distress was the alarm.
John Scott Haldane proposed this idea in 1895.
Canaries were used in mines as early as 1896.
Modern sensors have replaced the birds.
But the phrase 'canary in a coal mine' still warns us of hidden danger.

claims.claim: Canaries were used as early-warning signals for toxic gases, primarily carbon monoxide, because their rapid breathing rate, small size, and high metabolism caused them to succumb before miners.
The idea of placing a warm-blooded animal in a mine to detect carbon monoxide was first proposed by John Scott Haldane in 1895, and canaries were used as early as 1896.
Canaries would express signs of distress or collapse much earlier than other species, allowing coal workers to evacuate before the toxic gas reached a hazardous concentration.
Modern sensing equipment has replaced the use of small animals such as canaries in mines.
